#### Authentication file management

##### Upload an authentication file

The Data Integration service of DataWorks supports third-party identity authentication mechanisms. Before you use an authentication mechanism to perform identity authentication, you must upload the required authentication files on the Authentication File Management page of the DataWorks console. Then, you must enable third-party identity authentication when you add a data source. This way, only trusted applications and services can access the data source. This topic describes how to upload and reference an authentication file.

**Background information**

Third-party identity authentication mechanisms are used to perform strict identity authentication on users and services. These mechanisms prevent untrusted applications or services from accessing data and improve the security of data access during data synchronization. On the Authentication File Management page of the DataWorks console, you can manage authentication files in a centralized manner. You can upload an authentication file and view the data sources that reference the authentication file on this page.

**Limits**

DataWorks supports Kerberos and SSL authentication. For more information about how to configure Kerberos and SSL authentication, see the Configure Kerberos authentication and Configure SSL authentication. To use an identity authentication mechanism, you must upload the required authentication files on the Authentication File Management page of the DataWorks console.
1. Log in to the DataWorks console.
icon in the upper-left corner and choose **All Products**
**> Data Integration > Data Integration**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane of the Data Integration page, choose **Configuration**
**Options > Authentication File Management**.
4. On the **Authentication File Management** page, click **Upload Authentication File** in
the upper-right corner.
5. In the **Upload Authentication File** dialog box, click **Upload File**, select a file, and then
enter a description in the **File Description** field.
6. Click **OK**.

**Reference an authentication file**

**What to do next**

You can upload an authentication file and view the data sources that reference the uploaded authentication file on the **Authentication File Management** page. You can also remove multiple authentication files at a time.

##### Configure Kerberos authentication

The Data Integration service of DataWorks supports Kerberos authentication. After you configure Kerberos authentication, only trusted applications and services can pass identity authentication. This way, only the applications and services that pass the authentication can access data. This topic describes how Kerberos authentication works.

**Background information**

Kerberos is a computer network security protocol for authentication. It supports single sign-on (SSO). You need to provide your credentials only once to obtain a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT). Then, you can use the TGT to access multiple services. Kerberos provides high security. When you use Kerberos, a shared key is created between a trusted client and the server. Clients communicate with servers by using keys. This way, untrusted services or applications cannot access data.

**Limits**

For Apache Hadoop (CDH) clusters, only CDH 6.x clusters support Kerberos authentication. CDH clusters of other versions or self-managed CDH clusters for which Kerberos authentication tests are not performed may fail to pass the authentication.

**How Kerberos authentication works**

Kerberos is a third-party authentication protocol that is based on symmetric keys. Clients and servers use Key Distribution Center (KDC) to perform identity authentication. KDC is a server program of Kerberos and can distribute TGTs. The preceding figure shows the four stages of the Kerberos authentication on DataWorks.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Special Authentication Method | Set this parameter to Kerberos Authentication. |

1. A client requests a TGT: When a client (principal) accesses a data source for which
Kerberos authentication is enabled, the client requests a TGT from KDC.
2. KDC grants a TGT: After KDC receives a request from the client, KDC authenticates the
identity of the client. If the client passes the authentication, KDC grants an encrypted TGT that has a specific validity period to the client.
3. The client requests to access a specific service: After the client obtains the TGT, the client
requests to access specific service resources from the server based on the service name.
4. The service server authenticates the identity of the client: After the service server receives
the request from the client, the server authenticates the identity of the client. If the client passes the authentication, the client can access the service resources. A keytab authentication file and a krb5.conf configuration file are required for Kerberos authentication. The krb5.conf configuration file is used to store the configurations of KDC servers. The keytab file is used to store the identity authentication tickets of resource principals, including principals and encrypted principal keys. Before you perform Kerberos authentication, you must upload the keytab authentication file and keb5.conf file on the Authentication File Management page of the DataWorks console, and reference the uploaded files and configure a principal when you add a data source. For information about how to upload the required authentication files, see Upload an authentication file.

**Data source types that support Kerberos authentication**

For more information about the Kerberos data source types and configuration guidelines, see Configure an HBase data source, Configure a Hive data source, and Configure an HDFS data source.

**Reference an authentication file**

##### Configure SSL authentication

The data synchronization feature of DataWorks supports SSL authentication. Configuring SSL authentication ensures that only trusted applications and services can access your data resources. This topic describes the SSL authentication mechanism.

**Background information**

Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) authentication is a security protocol widely used in network communications. It establishes an encrypted link between a client and a server to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of data in transit. SSL authentication relies on a public key infrastructure (PKI), which uses digital certificates to authenticate the server, and sometimes the client, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks and identity spoofing. During the SSL authentication process, the server presents a digital certificate issued by a trusted certificate authority (CA) to the client to prove its identity. After the client validates the certificate, both parties use asymmetric encryption to negotiate a session key. Both parties then encrypt subsequent communication by using symmetric encryption, enabling efficient and secure data transfer. Common use cases include HTTPS website access, email transmission, and online payment systems. SSL and its successor, Transport Layer Security (TLS), create a secure channel over an insecure network to prevent data eavesdropping, tampering, and impersonation. As a result, they have become one of the cornerstones of modern secure network communication. As internet applications demand higher security, SSL authentication has become a critical technology to ensure service trustworthiness and protect user privacy. For the data source types that support SSL and their configuration guides, see Configure a PolarDB data source, Configure a MySQL data source, Configure an Oracle data source, Configure a PostgreSQL data source, Configure an SQL Server data source, Configure a TiDB data source, Configure a ClickHouse data source, and Configure a Hive data source.

**Referencing certificate files**

To use SSL authentication, select the SSL authentication method on the data source configuration page, configure the relevant parameters, and reference the required certificate files. The following section describes the key parameters for configuring SSL authentication for a MySQL data source. For details on configuring data sources, see Supported data sources.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| authentication method | Select SSL Authentication. |
| truststore certificate file | Select the uploaded truststore certificate file from the drop-down list. To upload a new certificate file, click Add Certificate File. |
| keystore certificate file | Select the uploaded keystore certificate file from the drop-down list. To upload a new certificate file, click Add Certificate File. |
| truststore password and keystore password | The passwords for the truststore and keystore certificate files. |

#### Configure processing rules for DDL

**messages**

The binary log messages of relational databases may contain DDL statements. On the Processing Policy for DDL Messages in Real-time Sync page, you can specify how the destination processes these DDL messages.

**Usage notes**

This policy takes effect by default only on the current project. When you create a solution with real-time synchronization configured, this policy is used by default.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the DataWorks console.
icon in the upper-left corner and choose **All Products**
**> Data Integration > Data Integration**.
3. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Configuration Options > Processing Policy for**
**DDL Messages in Real-time Sync**.
4. Select a data source from the **Synchronize To** drop-down list. The actual data sources
available in the console prevail.
5. Select a policy from the **CreateTable**, **DropTable**, **AddColumn**, **DropColumn**,
**RenameTable**, **RenameColumn**, **Modify Column**, and **TruncateTAble** drop-down lists.
The details of each processing policy are as follows: Normal: The system sends the DDL message to the destination. Then, the destination processes the DDL message. Different destinations respond to DDL messages in different ways. Ignore: The system discards the DDL message and no longer sends this message to the destination. Error: The system directly stops the real-time synchronization node by assigning an error status to the node.
6. Click **Save**.

#### Resource groups

##### Overview

This topic introduces the definition of resource groups. It also describes how the connectivity and performance of resource groups affect data synchronization.

**Definition**

A resource group is a collection of computing resources on which synchronization nodes of Data Integration are run. In most cases, a resource group is one or more servers that consist of CPU, memory, and network resources. In the process of running a synchronization node, the resource group pulls data from the source and pushes the data to the destination.

**Connectivity and performance**

When you use resource groups, you must pay attention to their connectivity and performance. To ensure that data can be synchronized, a resource group must be connected to the source and destination. Connectivity is the most important factor that affects data synchronization. Data Integration cannot build networks. Before you use Data Integration to synchronize data, you must make sure that the resource group is connected to the data sources. If the resource group is disconnected from the data sources, synchronization nodes cannot be run. Performance Synchronization nodes consume the CPU, memory, and network resources on the servers where the nodes are run. Insufficient resources may lead to various issues. For example, the nodes fail to be started, wait for resources for a long period of time after startup, transmit data at a low rate, or fail to generate data. To ensure the smooth running of synchronization nodes, you must allocate adequate resources for them.

##### Shared resource groups

Data Integration of DataWorks provides shared resource groups for you to create and run synchronization nodes. Shared resource groups for Data Integration are created and maintained by Data Integration. Shared resource groups compose a public resource pool. Nodes that use resources in the public resource pool may not be run as scheduled due to insufficient resources. We recommend that you prepare sufficient resources to ensure the efficient running of synchronization nodes.

**Note**

You can run a maximum of 25 parallel nodes on a shared resource group for Data Integration when the shared resource group is not in use. You cannot change the memory size of a shared resource group. Instead, you can change the number of parallel nodes that can be run on the shared resource group. The following formula is used to calculate the memory size: Memory size = `Number`

```
of parallel nodes × 512 MB .
```

## DataStudio

### Guidelines and specifications

**of SQL coding**

This topic describes the basic guidelines and detailed specifications of SQL coding.

**SQL coding guidelines**

When you write SQL code, take note of the following guidelines: The code is comprehensive. Code lines are clear, neat, well-organized, and structured. The optimal execution speed is considered during SQL coding. Comments need to be added if necessary to enhance the readability of your code. The guidelines impose non-mandatory constraints on the coding behavior of developers. In practice, understandable deviations are allowed when developers obey general rules. All SQL keywords and reserved words must be all uppercase or lowercase, such as select/SELECT, from/FROM, where/WHERE, and/AND, or/OR, union/UNION, insert/INSERT, delete/DELETE, group/GROUP, having/HAVING, and count/COUNT. Do not use mixed-case letters, such as Select or seLECT. A unit of indentation contains four spaces. All indentations must be the integral multiple of an indentation unit. The code is aligned based on its hierarchy. You cannot use an `asterisk (*)` to specify a column name. The column name must be specified for all statements. Matching opening and closing parentheses must be placed in the same column.

**SQL coding specifications**

When you write SQL code, take note of the following specifications: Code header The code header contains information such as the subject, description, author, and date. Reserve a line for change log and a title line so that users can add change records in the future. Each line can contain a maximum of 80 characters. The following code provides an example template:

```
--************************************************************************** -- ** Subject: Transaction -- ** Description: Transaction refund analysis -- ** Author: Youma -- ** Created on: 20170616 -- ** Change log: -- ** Modified on Modified by Content -- yyyymmdd name comment -- 20170831 Wuma Add a comment on the biz_type=1234 transaction --**************************************************************************
```

Field arrangement Use a line for each field that is selected for the SELECT statement. Reserve one unit of indentation between the word SELECT and the first selected field. Start each of the other field names in a new line with two units of indentation and a comma (,). Place the comma (,) between two fields right before the second field. Place the AS statement in the same line as its matching field and keep AS statements of multiple fields in the same column. Clause arrangement for an INSERT statement Arrange the clauses of an INSERT statement in the same line. The clauses such as **FROM**, **WHERE**, **GROUP BY**, **HAVING**, **ORDER BY**, **JOIN**, and **UNION** in a SELECT statement must be arranged in compliance with the following requirements: Use a line for each clause. The clauses are left aligned with the SELECT statement. Reserve two units of indentation between the first word of a clause and its content. Keep the logical operators such as **AND** and **OR** in a WHERE clause left aligned with the word WHERE. If the length of a clause name exceeds two units of indentation such as **ORDER BY** and
**GROUP BY**, add a space between the clause name and its content.
Spacing before and after operators Reserve one space before and after each arithmetic operator and logical operator. Keep all the operators in the same line unless the length of the code exceeds 80 characters. The SELECT CASE statement is used to evaluate the value of a variable. Take note of the following specifications on SELECT CASE statements: Write the WHEN clause one unit of indentation after the CASE statement in the same line. Use a line for each WHEN clause. Wrap a line if the clause is excessively long. The CASE statement must contain the ELSE clause. The ELSE clause must be aligned with the WHEN clause. Nested query Nested queries are often used to implement the extract, transform, and load (ETL) process of data warehouse systems. The following figure shows an example of arranging nested queries. Table alias If an alias is defined for a table in a SELECT statement, you must use the alias whenever you reference the table in the statement. Specify an alias for each table in the SELECT statement. We recommend that you define the table aliases by using letters in alphabetical order. In the nested query, levels 1 to 4 of SQL statements are named part, segment, unit, and detail, which are abbreviated as P, S, U, and D. You can also use a, b, c, and d to represent levels 1 to 4. To differentiate multiple clauses at the same level, add numbers such as 1, 2, 3, and 4after the letter that represents the level. SQL comments Add a comment for each SQL statement. Use a separate line for the comment of each SQL statement and place the comment in front of the SQL statement. Place the comment of a field right after the field. Add comments to clauses that are difficult to understand. Add a comment to important code. If a statement is long, we recommend that you add comments based on the purposes of each segment. The description for a constant or variable is required. The comment on the valid value range is optional.

**development in the code editor**

DataWorks provides features such as intelligent code hinting and built-in code templates. This topic describes how these features help improve the efficiency of code development in the code editor.

These features can help improve the efficiency of code development only for ODPS-based nodes, including ODPS SQL nodes and ODPS Script nodes.

icon and choose **All Products > Data**
**Development and O&M > DataStudio**. The **DataStudio** page appears.

**Intelligent code hinting**

#### Perform smoke testing

After you develop code, you must debug the code. This topic describes how to perform smoke testing in a development environment.

**Introduction to smoke testing**

Before you release a node, we recommend that you perform **smoke testing** to verity the configuration and execution logic of the node. It is usually used for the following purposes: Check whether the scheduling parameters of the node can be replaced without errors. Check whether the upstream and downstream dependencies of the node are correctly configured. Check whether the node execution result is as expected. For workspaces in standard mode, perform smoke testing in **an isolated development**
**environment**. This way, even if a node writes data during smoke testing, the data in the
production environment is not affected.

**Enable the forcible smoke testing feature**

The administrator of a workspace can enable the forcible smoke testing feature on the Settings page of DataStudio. If this feature is enabled, a node in the workspace must pass smoking testing before it can be deployed to the production environment. To enable the forcible smoke testing feature, perform the following steps:

**Note**

The forcible smoke testing feature is unavailable for workspaces in basic mode.
1. In the lower-right corner of the left-side navigation pane of DataStudio, click the
icon.
2. On the Settings page, choose **Security Settings and Others > Smoke Testing** and
enable forcible smoke testing. After you write code, you can use one of the following methods to perform smoke testing before you deploy and run a node: Method 1: When you commit a node, click the of the node. In the **Commit** dialog box, select **Yes** for **Smoke Testing**. Method 2: After you commit a node, click the of the node. In the **Smoke Testing** dialog box, configure the Data Timestamp parameter and click OK. Method 3: After you commit a node, click Deploy in the toolbar of the configuration tab of the node. On the **Create Deploy Task** page, click **Smoke Testing** in the Actions column. Method 4: In the upper part of the DataStudio page, click Operation Center. In the upperleft corner of the **Operation Center** page, switch to the development environment. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Cycle Task Maintenance > Cycle Task**. In the rightside list, click **Test** in the Actions column of the desired node.

3. On the Smoke Testing Records page, you can click **View Logs** in the Actions column to
view the execution details of a specific smoke testing instance. You can click **Stop** in the Actions column to stop a smoke testing instance for which the value of **Status** is **Running**.

#### Data lineage

Data lineage shows the relationships between a node and other nodes. It includes two parts: a dependency graph and an internal lineage graph.
1. Log on to the DataWorks console.
2. Double-click the target node. For more information about creating a node, see ODPS SQL
node.
3. On the right side of the editor, click **Lineage**.
**Data Lineage** includes **Dependency Graph** and **Internal Lineage Graph**.

**Dependency graph**

Use the dependency graph to verify that the node's dependencies are configured as expected. If not, you can return to the scheduling configuration page to modify them.

**Internal lineage graph**

The internal lineage graph is generated by parsing the node's code.

```
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE dw_user_info_all_d PARTITION (dt='${bdp.system.bizdate}')
  , b.gender
  , b.age_range
  , b.zodiac
  , a.region
  , a.device
  , a.identity
  , a.method
  , a.url
  , a.referer
  , a.time
FROM (
  FROM ods_log_info_d
  WHERE dt = ${bdp.system.bizdate}
) a LEFT OUTER JOIN (
  FROM ods_user_info_d
  WHERE dt = ${bdp.system.bizdate}
) b ON a.uid = b.uid;
```

The preceding SQL code generates the following internal lineage graph.

#### Versions

The Versions tab displays the version information that is generated each time a node is committed and deployed. You can view the historical versions and information about each version. The information includes the user that committed the node, time when the node was committed, change type, status, and description.

**Note**

Only a committed node has version information. Each time a node is committed, a version is generated and added to the **Versions** tab.
1. Log in to the DataWorks console.
2. On the **DataStudio** page, double-click the desired node.

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| Versions | The version of the API. A version is generated each time the API is published. v1 indicates version 1, and v2 indicates version 2. The version number increases by 1 each time a new version is generated. |
| File ID | The ID of the current node. |
| Committed By | The user that committed the node. |
| Committed At | The time when the version was committed. If a version is committed and then published, the value of this parameter is updated to the time when the version is published. By default, this column displays the time when the version is last published. |
| Change Type | The operation that is performed on the node. The first time that the node is committed and deployed, the value of this parameter is Create. However, if the node is modified, committed, and then deployed, the value of this parameter is Change. |
| Actions | The actions that you can perform on the version. The following actions are available: View, Compare, and Roll Back. View: Click the button to view the code of the current version. Compare: Click the button to compare the code and properties between two selected versions. You can compare a saved version with a committed version. Roll Back: Click the button to roll back the node from the current version to the desired version. After you roll back a node, you must commit and deploy it again. |

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| Saved At | The time when the node was saved. |
| File ID | The ID of the current node. |
| Saved By | The user who saved the node. |

3. On the node configuration tab that appears, click **Versions** in the right-side navigation
pane. On the Versions tab, view **Submitted Version** and **Saved Versions** of the current node. Committed versions:
**Saved versions**:

| Actions | The actions that you can perform on the version. The following actions are available: View, Compare, and Roll Back. View: Click the button to view the code of the current version. Compare: Click the button to compare the code and properties between two selected versions. You can compare a saved version with a committed version. Roll Back: Click the button to roll back the node from the current version to the desired version. After you roll back a node, you must commit and deploy it again. |
|---|---|

#### Code structure

The Code Structure tab displays the SQL code structure parsed from the code of a node. The code structure helps you view and modify the code.

MaxCompute SQL node, see Create an ODPS SQL node.

navigation pane. In this example, the MaxCompute SQL node contains the following SQL statement:

```
INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE dw_user_info_all_d PARTITION (dt='${bdp.system.bizdate}')
  , b.gender
  , b.age_range
  , b.zodiac
  , a.region
  , a.device
  , a.identity
  , a.method
  , a.url
  , a.referer
  , a.time
FROM (
  FROM ods_log_info_d
  WHERE dt = ${bdp.system.bizdate}
) a LEFT OUTER JOIN (
  FROM ods_user_info_d
  WHERE dt = ${bdp.system.bizdate}
) b ON a.uid = b.uid;
```

The following code structure is parsed from the preceding SQL statement. You can switch between the classic and outline modes. Move the pointer over a circle to view the description.
**Source table**: the table to be queried.
**Filter**: the condition for filtering the partitions in the table to be queried.
**Intermediate table (query view)**: the first temporary table that stores the query
results.
**Association (join)**: the operation for joining the query results.
**Intermediate table (query view)**: the second temporary table that stores the results of
the JOIN operation. This temporary table can be stored for three days. After three days, this table is automatically deleted.

### Business flows

#### Overview

DataWorks organizes different types of nodes in a workflow by business category. This allows you to develop code by business. DataWorks provides dashboards for different types of nodes in each workflow and provides tools for you to optimize and manage nodes in each workflow. This implements easy, intelligent development and management.

**Workflow structure**

A workspace supports various types of compute engines and can contain multiple workflows. A workflow is a collection of various types of nodes that are tightly associated with each other. DataWorks automatically generates a directed acyclic graph (DAG) for the workflow so that you can view the workflow. A workflow supports the following types of nodes: data integration, data analytics, table, resource, function, and algorithm. Each node is stored in an independent folder. You can create subfolders in each folder. To manage nodes in an efficient manner, we recommend that you create up to four levels of subfolders. If you create more than four levels of subfolders, your workflow becomes excessively complex. In this case, we recommend that you split your workflow into two or more workflows and add the workflows to the same solution to improve work efficiency.
1. Log in to the DataWorks console.
2. In the upper-left corner of the console, click the
icon and choose **All Products > Data**
**Development and O&M > DataStudio**. Then, the **DataStudio** page appears.
3. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
4. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, configure the **Workflow Name** and **Description**
parameters.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
5. Click **Create**.

**Composition of a manually triggered workflow**

**Note**

We recommend that you create no more than 100 nodes in a manually triggered workflow. A manually triggered workflow consists of nodes of the following modules. After you create a manually triggered workflow, open this workflow and create nodes of various types for each module. Double-click **Data Integration** under a manually triggered workflow to view all the Data Integration nodes in the workflow. Right-click **Data Integration** and choose **Create Node > Offline synchronization** to create an offline synchronization node. For more information, see Create a batch sync node. Right-click **Hologres** and choose **Create Node > Hologres SQL** to create a Hologres SQL node. For more information, see Create a Hologres SQL node. The MaxCompute compute engine allows you to create data analytics nodes such as ODPS SQL, SQL Snippet, ODPS Spark, PyODPS, ODPS Script, and ODPS MR nodes. You can also view and create tables, resources, and functions.

**Data Analytics**

Click **MaxCompute** under a manually triggered workflow and right-click **Table** to create a table. You can also view all the tables that are created in the current MaxCompute compute engine instance. For more information, see Create a MaxCompute table. Click **MaxCompute** under a manually triggered workflow and right-click **Resource** to create a resource. You can also view all the resources that are created in the current MaxCompute compute engine. For more information, see Create, reference, and download resources. Right-click **Algorithm** under a manually triggered workflow to create a Platform for AI (PAI) node. You can also view all the PAI nodes that are created in the current manually triggered workflow. **View all workflows**

**View the dashboard for each type of node**

DataWorks provides a dashboard for each type of node in a workflow. On the dashboard, each node is presented by a card that offers operation and optimization suggestions. This way, you can intelligently manage nodes. For example, the card of each data analytics node provides two indicators to show whether baseline-based monitoring and event notification are enabled for the node. This allows you to understand the status of each node. You can double-click a folder in a workflow to view the dashboard of the selected node type.

If you have modified the code or properties of a node but you have not committed the node on the configuration tab of the node, you can select the node in the Commit dialog box. Then, you can enter your comments in the **Change Description** field and click **Confirm**. The modification to the code or properties of the node is committed.

#### Create and reference a node group

This topic describes how to create and reference a node group.

**Background information**

You can group several nodes that are frequently reused together as a node group. The configuration of each node remains unchanged after the nodes are added to a node group. Later, you can directly reference the node group to reuse these nodes.

**Create a node group**

1. Log in to the DataWorks console.
2. In the upper-left corner of the console, click the
icon and choose **All Products > Data**
**Development and O&M > DataStudio**. The **DataStudio** page appears.
3. On the **DataStudio** page, create a workflow. For more information, see the Create a
workflow section of the Overview topic.
4. Go to the workflow configuration tab and click the
icon in the upper-right corner. Then, select the nodes that you want to add to the node group.
5. Right-click a node among the selected nodes and click **New Node Group**.
6. In the **New Node Group** dialog box, specify **Name** and click **OK**.
7. Right-click the node group and select **Save node group**. In the dialog box that appears,
click OK. Then, you can view the created node group in the **Node Group** section.

| Operation | Description |
|---|---|
| Save node group | Save the node group. The node group that you have created appears in the Node Group section only after you click Save node group. A node group that is not saved cannot be referenced in other workflows. |
| Delete node group | Delete the node group. Click Delete node group to delete all nodes in the selected node group. |
| Split node group | Dismiss the node group. After the node group is dismissed, the selected nodes no longer belong to a node group in the workflow. However, the node group still exists in the node group list. |

**Note**

If the created node group contains a Platform for AI (PAI) node, create a PAI experiment in another workflow to reference the node group. If the created node group contains a branch node, add digits to the value in the
**Associated Node Output** parameter. For more information, see Create a
branch node. You can directly drag a node group to another workflow to reference the node group in the workflow. The dependencies among the nodes in the node group remain unchanged. You can run the workflow or commit and deploy the workflow. Then, go to **Operation Center** to view the execution result.

#### Manually triggered workflows

In a manually triggered workflow, all nodes must be manually triggered. They cannot be automatically scheduled by DataWorks. Therefore, you do not need to specify parent nodes or output for nodes in manually triggered workflows.

**Create a manually triggered workflow**

1. Log in to the DataWorks console.
2. In the upper-left corner of the console, click the
icon and choose **All Products > Data**
**Development and O&M > DataStudio**. The **DataStudio** page appears.

icon, right-click **Manually Triggered**
**Workflows**, and select **Create Workflow**.

parameters.

**Note**

The workflow name must be 1 to 128 characters in length, and can contain letters, digits, underscores (_), and periods (.).
5. Click **Create**.

We recommend that you create no more than 100 nodes in a single manually triggered workflow.

### Node development

#### Table Management

##### Batch synchronization node

Batch synchronization nodes support various types of data sources, such as MaxCompute, MySQL, PolarDB-X, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle, MongoDB, Db2, Tablestore, Object Storage Service (OSS), FTP, HBase, LogHub, Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS), and Stream.

**Background information**

When you enter a table name, a drop-down list appears, displaying all matching tables. Only exact match is supported. Therefore, you must enter a complete table name. Tables are labeled as **Unsupported** if they are not supported by batch synchronization nodes. If you move the pointer over a table in the list, the details of the table are displayed, such as the database, IP address, and owner of the table. The details help you select the correct table. After you select and click a table, the column information is automatically specified. You can add, move, or remove columns. A data source for batch synchronization is created. You must add your database to DataWorks as a data source before you can use the data source to access data in the database. For more information about how to create a data source, see Supported data sources.

**Step 1: Create a batch synchronization task**

1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the workflow and choose **Create Node > Data Integration > Offline**
**synchronization**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

For more information about how to configure a batch synchronization task, see Configure data synchronization tasks.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node.

#### MaxCompute

##### ODPS SQL node

ODPS SQL uses an SQL-like syntax and is designed for distributed processing of massive datasets (terabyte-scale) where real-time performance is not critical.

**Background**

Each job takes significant time to complete its lifecycle, from preparation to submission. This makes ODPS SQL ideal for online analytical processing (OLAP) applications that prioritize high throughput for tasks involving thousands or tens of thousands of transactions. The MaxCompute directory appears on the current page only after you add a MaxCompute compute engine instance on the **Workspace Configurations** page. For more information, see Bind a MaxCompute compute engine.

**Limitations**

ODPS SQL does not support running `set` , `use` , or `alias` statements independently. They must be executed together with other SQL statements. For example:

```
SET a=b; CREATE TABLE name(id string);
```

ODPS SQL does not support adding comments immediately after a keyword statement such as `set` , `use` , or `alias` . For example:

```
CREATE TABLE name(id string); SET a=b; -- This comment is not supported. CREATE TABLE name1(id string)；
```

The execution behavior differs between Data Development and scheduled runs: Data Development: Merges all keyword statements ( `set` , `use` , and `alias` ) in the task code and places them before all other SQL statements. Scheduled runs: Execute statements sequentially.

```
SET a=b; CREATE TABLE name1(id string); SET c=d; CREATE TABLE name2(id string);
```

The following table shows the execution results.

| Second SQL statement | SET a=b; SET c=d; CREATE TABLE name2(id string); | SET c=d; CREATE TABLE name2(id string); |
|---|---|---|

A scheduling parameter must be in the `key=value` format. Do not use spaces before or after the equals sign (=). For example:

```
time={yyyymmdd hh:mm:ss} --Incorrect. a =b --Incorrect.
```

If you use keywords such as `bizdate` or `date` as scheduling parameter variables, the format must be `yyyymmdd` . To use other formats, choose a different variable name to avoid conflicts. For example:

```
bizdate=201908 --Incorrect. This format is not supported.
```

In **Data Development**, to return a query result, your SQL statement must begin with `select` , `read` , or `with` . Otherwise, it generates no output. When executing multiple SQL statements, separate them with a semicolon (;) and place each statement on a new line. Incorrect example

```
CREATE table1;CREATE table2
```

Correct example

```
CREATE table1; CREATE table2;
```

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the target workflow and choose **Create Node > MaxCompute > ODPS SQL**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Develop the ODPS SQL task**

After creating the node, write your ODPS SQL code. The following example shows how to create a table, insert data into it, and query the results:
1. Create a table named test1.

```
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS test1 ( id BIGINT COMMENT '' ,
  name STRING COMMENT '' ,
  age BIGINT COMMENT '' ,
  sex STRING COMMENT ''
  );
```

2. Insert the prepared data.

```
INSERT INTO test1 VALUES (1,'Zhang San',43,'Male') ; INSERT INTO test1 VALUES (1,'Li Si',32,'Male') ; INSERT INTO test1 VALUES (1,'Chen Xia',27,'Female') ; INSERT INTO test1 VALUES (1,'Wang Wu',24,'Male') ; INSERT INTO test1 VALUES (1,'Ma*',35,'Female') ; INSERT INTO test1 VALUES (1,'Zhao*',22,'Female') ; INSERT INTO test1 VALUES (1,'Zhou Zhuang',55,'Male') ;
```

3. Query the table data.

```
SELECT * FROM test1;
```

##### SQL component node

An SQL component is an SQL code template that includes multiple input and output parameters. It generates a new target table by referencing source tables and performing operations such as filtering, joining, and aggregation.

**Background**

After a component developer publishes a new version, users can upgrade their component instances to the latest version. Component versioning lets developers continuously upgrade components, improving workflow execution efficiency and optimizing business outcomes. For example, User A uses version V1 of a component owned by User B. If User B upgrades the component to V2, User A can continue to use V1 but sees an update notification. After comparing the old and new code, if User A finds that the new version delivers better business results, they can upgrade to the new version. When upgrading an SQL component node developed from a component template, click
**Update Code Version** and then confirm that the parameter configuration for the new
version remains valid. After you make the necessary adjustments based on the new version's description, the process is the same as for a standard SQL node: save, commit, and publish. You have added a MaxCompute compute engine instance on the **Workspace**

##### PyODPS 2 node

DataWorks provides the PyODPS 2 node type, which integrates the Python SDK for MaxCompute. You can directly edit Python code in a DataWorks PyODPS 2 node to interact with MaxCompute.

**Background**

MaxCompute provides a Python SDK that you can use to access and manage MaxCompute.

**Note**

The underlying Python version for a PyODPS 2 node is 2.7. A PyODPS 2 node can process a maximum of 50 MB of data locally and consume no more than 1 GB of memory during runtime. If these limits are exceeded, the task is terminated. Avoid writing data-intensive processing code in PyODPS 2 nodes. For pure Python code, use a Shell node to run Python scripts that you have uploaded to DataWorks. The MaxCompute directory is displayed only after you add a MaxCompute compute engine instance on the **Workspace Settings** page. For more information, see Bind a MaxCompute compute engine.
1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the target business workflow and select **New Node > MaxCompute >**
**PyODPS 2**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Develop PyODPS 2 task**

Go to the PyODPS 2 edit page and start editing.
1. Enter the ODPS entry point.
In a DataWorks PyODPS 2 node, DataWorks provides the global variables **odps** and o as the ODPS entry point. You do not need to define it manually.

```python
print(odps.exist_table('PyODPS_iris'))
```

2. Execute SQL.
PyODPS 2 nodes support ODPS SQL queries and allow you to read the execution results. The **execute_sql** or **run_sql** method returns an instance object. Not all commands available in the MaxCompute client are supported SQL statements in PyODPS. To call statements other than Data Definition Language (DDL) or Data Manipulation Language (DML), use other methods. For example, to execute statements such as GRANT or REVOKE, use the
**run_security_query** method. For PAI commands, use the **run_xflow** or
**execute_xflow** method.

```python
o.execute_sql('select * from dual') # Executes synchronously and blocks until the SQ L execution is complete. instance = o.run_sql('select * from dual') # Executes asynchronously. print(instance.get_logview_address()) # Gets the Logview address. instance.wait_for_success() # Blocks until the execution is complete.
```

3. Set the runtime parameters.
You can set runtime parameters by using the **hints** parameter, which is a **dict**.

```
o.execute_sql('select * from PyODPS_iris', hints={'odps.sql.mapper.split.size': 16})
```

If you configure global settings with **sql.settings**, PyODPS automatically applies these settings as hints to every SQL execution.

```python
from odps import options options.sql.settings = {'odps.sql.mapper.split.size': 16} o.execute_sql('select * from PyODPS_iris') # Hints are added based on the global con figuration.
```

4. Read the SQL execution results.
An instance returned by an SQL execution can directly call the **open_reader** operation. This applies in the following two scenarios: The SQL statement returns structured data.

```
with o.execute_sql('select * from dual').open_reader() as reader: for record in reader: # Process each record.
```

When you run an SQL statement such as desc, use the **reader.raw** attribute to get the raw SQL output.

```
with o.execute_sql('desc dual').open_reader() as reader:
```

**Note**

If you use custom scheduling parameters, you must hardcode the time values when you run the PyODPS node directly from the editor page. The node cannot automatically substitute these parameters.

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node.

**Step 4: Debug the node code**

**Parameters** dialog box, select a resource group for scheduling that you want to use to
debug the code. If you use scheduling parameters in your code, assign the scheduling parameters to variables as values in the node code for debugging.

You can perform smoke testing on the node in the development environment when you commit the node or after you commit the node. For more information, see Perform smoke testing. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.

##### PyODPS 3 node

DataWorks provides the PyODPS 3 node, which allows you to write MaxCompute jobs directly in Python and schedule them to run periodically. This topic describes how to configure and schedule Python jobs in DataWorks. The MaxCompute directory is displayed only after you add a MaxCompute compute engine instance on the **workspace configuration** page. For more information, see Bind a MaxCompute compute engine.
1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the target business process and select **Create Node > MaxCompute >**
**PyODPS 3**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Develop PyODPS 3 task**

Edit the task in the PyODPS 3 editor.
1. ODPS entry point
In a DataWorks PyODPS node, a global variable, **odps** or o, serves as the ODPS entry point. You do not need to define it manually.

```python
print(odps.exist_table('PyODPS_iris'))
```

2. Execute SQL
You can execute SQL statements in a PyODPS node. By default, **instance tunnel** is disabled in DataWorks. This means that
**instance.open_reader** uses the Result API, which can retrieve a maximum of 10,000
records. You can use **reader.count** to retrieve the number of records. If you need to iterate through and retrieve all data, you must disable the `limit` . To enable Instance Tunnel globally and disable the `limit` , use the following statements:

```bash
options.tunnel.use_instance_tunnel = True options.tunnel.limit_instance_tunnel = False # Disable the limit to read all data. with instance.open_reader() as reader:
  # All data can be read through the Instance Tunnel.
```

You can also add `tunnel=True` to **open_reader** to enable the **instance tunnel** only for this **open_reader** call. Additionally, you can add `limit=False` to disable the `limit` restriction only for this call.

```bash
# Use the Instance Tunnel interface for this open_reader call and read all data.
with instance.open_reader(tunnel=True, limit=False) as reader:
```

You can set runtime parameters with the **hints** parameter, which is a **dict**.

```
o.execute_sql('select * from PyODPS_iris', hints={'odps.sql.mapper.split.size': 16}
```

) If you configure **sql.settings** globally, the specified runtime parameters apply to every execution.

```python
from odps import options options.sql.settings = {'odps.sql.mapper.split.size': 16} o.execute_sql('select * from PyODPS_iris') # Add hints based on the global configu ration.
```

4. Read execution results
You can directly call the **open_reader** operation on the instance that runs an SQL statement. There are two scenarios: The SQL statement returns structured data.

```
with o.execute_sql('select * from dual').open_reader() as reader:
 for record in reader:  # Process each record.
```

If you run an SQL statement such as `desc` , you can use the **reader.raw** property to retrieve the raw execution result.

```
with o.execute_sql('desc dual').open_reader() as reader:
```

**Note**

If you use custom scheduling parameters, you must provide static values for them when you manually run a PyODPS 3 node in the editor. The node does not automatically substitute the variables.

2. Save and run the code.
In the top toolbar, click the icon to save node code and click the icon to run node code.
3. Optional. Perform smoke testing.
You can perform smoke testing on the node in the development environment when you commit the node or after you commit the node. For more information, see Perform smoke testing. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. In the top toolbar, click the
icon to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. If you use a workspace in standard mode, you must deploy the node to the production environment after you commit the node. To deploy a node, click **Deploy** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the node. For more information, see Deploy nodes.

**What to do next**

Task O&M: After you commit and deploy the node, the node is periodically run based on the scheduling configurations. You can click **Operation Center** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the corresponding node to go to Operation Center and view the scheduling status of the node. For more information, see Auto triggered node O&M.

**Script Mode syntax and limits**

In Script Mode, SQL compilation is straightforward. You can write your script based on business logic much like a conventional programming language, without needing to organize the statement structure.

```
--SET statements set odps.sql.type.system.odps2=true; [set odps.stage.reducer.num=***;] [...] --DDL statements create table table1 xxx; [create table table2 xxx;] [...] --DML statements @var1 := SELECT [ALL | DISTINCT] select_expr, select_expr, ...
    FROM table3
    [WHERE where_condition];
@var2 := SELECT [ALL | DISTINCT] select_expr, select_expr, ...
    FROM table4
    [WHERE where_condition];
@var3 := SELECT [ALL | DISTINCT] var1.select_expr, var2.select_expr, ...
    FROM @var1 join @var2 on ...;
INSERT OVERWRITE|INTO TABLE [PARTITION (partcol1=val1, partcol2=val2 ...)]
    SELECT [ALL | DISTINCT] select_expr, select_expr, ...
    FROM @var3;
[@var4 := SELECT [ALL | DISTINCT] var1.select_expr, var.select_expr, ... FROM @var1
    SELECT [ALL | DISTINCT] var1.select_expr, var.select_expr, ... FROM @var2;
CREATE [EXTERNAL] TABLE [IF NOT EXISTS] table_name
```

`AS`

```
    SELECT [ALL | DISTINCT] select_expr, select_expr, ...
    FROM var4;]
```

The following list describes the syntax of Script Mode:

| CREATE TABLE AS |  | stateme |
|---|---|---|
| end writing |  |  |

Script Mode supports SET statements, some DDL statements, and all DML statements. DDL statements that display results on the screen, such as `desc` and `show` , are not supported. A script must follow the order of SET statements > DDL statements > DML statements. Each type can contain zero or more statements, and these statement types cannot be interleaved. Statements that start with an at sign ( @ ) assign their results to a variable. A script can contain a maximum of one statement that displays results on the screen, such as a standalone `SELECT` statement. Including more than one will cause an error. We recommend that you avoid using screen-displaying `SELECT` statements in scripts. statements separately. In Script Mode, if any statement fails, the entire script fails. In Script Mode, a job is created to process data only after all input data is ready. In Script Mode, an error occurs if you try to read from a table after writing to it in the same script.

```
insert overwrite table src2 select * from src where key > 0; @a := select * from src2; select * from @a;
```

To avoid this read-after-write error, modify the script as follows:

```
@a := select * from src where key > 0; insert overwrite table src2 select * from @a; select * from @a;
```

Example:

```
create table if not exists dest(key string , value bigint) partitioned by (d string); create table if not exists dest2(key string,value bigint ) partitioned by (d string); @a := select * from src where value >0; @b := select * from src2 where key is not null; @c := select * from src3 where value is not null; @d := select a.key,b.value from @a left outer join @b on a.key=b.key and b.value>0; @e := select a.key,c.value from @a inner join @c on a.key=c.key; @f := select * from @d union select * from @e union select * from @a; insert overwrite table dest partition (d='20171111') select * from @f; @g := select e.key,c.value from @e join @c on e.key=c.key; insert overwrite table dest2 partition (d='20171111') SELECT * from @g;
```

**When to use Script Mode**

Script Mode is ideal for rewriting a single statement with deeply nested subqueries, or for complex scripts that must be split into multiple statements due to their complexity. If your data sources have significantly different data readiness times (for example, one is ready at 1:00 AM and another at 7:00 AM), avoid using table parameters to combine separate SQL statements into a single, large Script Mode script.

##### Create a MaxCompute table

This topic describes how to create a MaxCompute table.

**Limits**

DataWorks does not allow you to create MaxCompute foreign tables in a visualized manner.

**Procedure**

1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the created workflow and choose **Create Table > MaxCompute > Table**.
You can also find the workflow that you want to use, right-click **MaxCompute**, and then select **Create Table**.

**Important**

The MaxCompute folder is displayed on the DataStudio page only after you associate a MaxCompute compute engine instance with the current workspace on the **Workspace**
**Management** page.
3. In the **Create Table** dialog box, configure the **Path** and **Name** parameters, and click
**Create**.

**Important**

The table name cannot exceed 64 characters in length. The table name must start with a letter and cannot contain special characters.
4. On the table configuration tab that appears, configure the parameters in the **General**
section.

| Level-1 Theme | The name of the level-1 folder in which the table resides. Note The level-1 and level-2 folders show the table locations in DataWorks to help you easily manage tables. |
|---|---|
| Level-2 Theme | The name of the level-2 folder in which the table resides. |
| Create Folder | Click Create Folder to go to the Folder Management tab. On the Folder Management tab, you can create level-1 and level-2 folders. |
| Descriptio n | The description of the table. |

| Section | Parameter | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Physical Model | Partition Type | The partition type of the table. Valid values: Partitioned Table and Non-Partitioned Table. |
|  | TTL | Specifies whether to enable the time-to-live (TTL) feature for the table. If you enable the TTL feature, you must enter a number in the TTL (Days) field. If the table or partition is stored for more than the specified number of days, data that has not been updated is deleted. |
|  | Level | The layer where the table data is stored or processed. A data warehouse consists of the operational data store (ODS), common data model (CDM), and application data service (ADS) layers. You can specify a name for each layer. |

5. Create a table.
You can use one of the following methods to create a table: Create a table by using a DDL statement. Click **DDL** in the top toolbar. In the dialog box that appears, enter the statement for creating a table. After you finish editing the statement, click **Generate Table Schema**. Information is automatically entered in the General, Physical Model, and Schema sections. Create a table on the GUI. If a DDL statement is inappropriate for you to create a table, try using the GUI. The following table describes the relevant parameters for creating a table on the GUI.

|  | Category | The business category to which the table belongs. Tables are categorized into the basic, advanced, and other-purpose business categories. You can specify a name for each business category. If you want to create a table category or level, click Create Level to go to the Level Management tab. Note Business categories are designed only to help you manage the table and do not affect underlying implementation. |
|---|---|---|
|  | Table Type | The type of the table. Default value: Internal Table. |
|  | Field Name | The name of the field. The name can contain letters, digits, and underscores ( ). _ |
|  | Display Name | The display name of the field. |
|  | Data Type | The data type of the field. |
|  | Definition or Maximum Value Length | The maximum value length of the field. You can specify the maximum value length only for fields of the DECIMAL, VARCHAR, ARRAY, MAP, and STRUCT types. |
|  | Description | The description of the field. |
|  | Primary Key Field | Specifies whether the field serves as the primary key or part of a composite primary key. |
|  | Create Field | Adds a field to the table. |

| Schema |  |  |
|---|---|---|
|  | Delete | Deletes an existing field from the table. Note If you want to delete a field from an existing table and then commit the table, you must delete the table and create another table that has the same name. You are not allowed to perform this operation in the production environment. |
|  | Move Up | Adjusts the field sequence of the table. If you want to adjust the sequence of fields in an existing table, you must delete the table and create another table that has the same name. You are not allowed to adjust the sequence of fields in an existing table in the production environment. |
|  | Move Down | Same as the Move Up operation. |
|  | Add | Adds a partition to the table. If you want to add a partition to an existing table and then commit the table, you must delete the table and create another table that has the same name. You are not allowed to add a partition to an existing table in the production environment. |
|  | Delete | Deletes a partition from the table. If you want to delete a partition from an existing table and then commit the table, you must delete the table and create another table with the same name. You are not allowed to add a partition to an existing table in the production environment. |
|  | Operation | Commits a partition or deletes a field. |

| Partition field design Note This section appears only when you set the Partition Type parameter to Partitioned Table in the Physical Model section. | Add | Adds a partition field. Note This button is displayed only when you create a partitioned table. |
|---|---|---|
|  | Data Type | The data type of the partition field. We recommend that you use the STRING type for all partition fields. |
|  | Length | The maximum length of the partition field. You can specify the maximum length only for fields of the VARCHAR type. |
|  | Description | The description of the partition field. |
|  | Partition Column Date Format | The format of the date partition. If the partition field is a date, although the data type may be STRING, select or enter a date format, such as yyyymmdd or yyyy- mm-dd. |
|  | Partition Column Date Granularity | The granularity of the date partition. The granularity can be second, minute, hour, day, month, quarter, or year. You can enter a partition granularity based on your business requirements. If you want to add multiple partitions with different granularities, take note that a greater granularity corresponds to a higher partition level. For example, three partitions whose granularities are day, hour, and month are available. Multi-level partitions are in the hierarchical order of level-1 partition (month), level-2 partition (day), and level-3 partition (hour). |

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|

6. Click **Commit to Development Environment** and **Commit to Production Environment**
in sequence. If the workspace that you use is in basic mode, you need only to click **Commit to**
**Production Environment**.

| Load from Development Environment | If the table has been committed to the development environment, this button is clickable. After you click this button, the information about the table you create in the development environment overwrites the table information on the current page. Note This feature is supported only for MaxCompute tables. |
|---|---|
| Commit to Development Environment | Before you click this button, make sure that you have configured all required parameters on the current page. You cannot click this button if any parameter is not configured. |
| Load from Production Environment | After you click this button, the information about the table that is committed to the production environment overwrites the table information on the current page. Note This feature is supported only for MaxCompute tables. |
| Commit to Production Environment | After you click this button, the table is created in the workspace of the production environment. |

After the table is created, you can query data in the table and modify or delete the table. For more information, see Manage tables.

##### Create and reference resources

This topic describes how to create and reference a JAR or Python resource.

**Background information**

If your code or function requires resource files such as**.jar** files, you can upload resources to your workspace and reference them. If the existing built-in functions do not meet your requirements, you can create user-defined functions (UDFs) and customize processing logic. You can upload the required JAR packages to your workspace so that you can reference them when you create UDFs.

**Note**

You can view built-in functions in the **Built-In Functions** pane. For more information, see View built-in functions. You can view the UDFs that you have committed or deployed on the **MaxCompute**
**Functions** tab.
You can upload different types of resources including text files, MaxCompute tables, Python code, and compressed packages in the **.zip**, **.tgz**, **.tar.gz**, **.tar**, and **.jar** formats to MaxCompute. You can read or use these resources when you run UDFs or MapReduce jobs. MaxCompute provides API operations for you to read and use resources. The following types of resources are supported:
**Python**: the Python code you have written. You can use Python code to register Python
UDFs.
**JAR**: the compiled Java JAR packages.
**Archive**: the compressed files that can be identified by the file name extension. Supported
file types include **.zip**, **.tgz**, **.tar.gz**, **.tar**, and **.jar**.
**File**: the files in the **.zip**, **.so**, or **.jar** format.
**JAR** resources and **file** resources have the following differences:
You can write Java code in an offline Java environment, compress the code to a JAR package, and then upload the package as a JAR resource to DataWorks. You can create and edit a small-sized file resource in the DataWorks console. If you want to upload a file resource whose size is greater than 500 KB from your onpremises machine when you create a file resource, you can select **Upload On-premises**
**Document**.

**Note**

Each resource to be uploaded cannot exceed 30 MB.

**Create a JAR resource**

1. Log in to the DataWorks console.
2. Move the pointer over the
**JAR**.
You can also find the workflow that you want to use, right-click **MaxCompute**, and then choose **Create Resource > JAR**.

**Important**

The MaxCompute folder is displayed on the DataStudio page only after you associate a MaxCompute compute engine instance with the current workspace on the **Workspace**
**Management** page.
3. In the **Create Resource** dialog box, configure the **Path** and **Name** parameters.

**Note**

The resource name can be different from the name of the uploaded file. The resource name must be 1 to 128 characters in length and can contain letters, digits, underscores (_), and periods (.). The name is not case-sensitive. A JAR resource name must end with **.jar**, and a Python resource name must end with **.py**.
4. Click **Upload** and select the file that you want to upload.
5. Click **Create**.
6. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save and commit the resource to the server for task scheduling and development.

**Create a Python resource and register a function**

1. Create a Python resource.
i. On the **DataStudio** page, move the pointer over the icon and choose **Create**
**Resource > MaxCompute > Python**.
You can also find the workflow that you want to use, right-click **MaxCompute**, and then choose **Create Resource > Python**. ii. In the **Create Resource** dialog box, configure the **Path** and **Name** parameters. iii. Click **Create**. iv. Write code for the created Python resource in the code editor. Sample code:

```python
from odps.udf import annotate @annotate("string->bigint") class ipint(object):
    def evaluate(self, ip):
        try:
            return reduce(lambda x, y: (x << 8) + y, map(int, ip.split('.')))
        except:
            return 0
```

v. Click the icon in the top toolbar.
2. Register a function.
i. On the **DataStudio** page, move the pointer over the icon and choose **Create**
**Function > MaxCompute**.
You can also find the workflow that you want to use, right-click **MaxCompute**, and then select **Create Solution**. ii. In the **Create Function** dialog box, configure the **Path** and **Name** parameters. iii. Click **Create**. iv. In the **Register Function** section of the configuration tab that appears, enter the class name and the name of the Python resource that has been created, and then click the icon in the toolbar. In this example, the class name is `ipint.ipint` . v. Check whether the **ipint** function is valid and meets your expectations. For example, you can create an ODPS SQL node to test the ipint function by running an SQL statement.

**Reference a resource**

For more information about how to reference a resource in a function, see Register a function. For more information about how to reference a resource in a node, see ODPS MR node.

##### Register a function

DataWorks supports Python and Java APIs. This topic describes how to register a function.

| Engine Instance MaxCompute | The MaxCompute compute engine instance. The value of this parameter cannot be changed. |
| Function Name | The name of the function. You can use the function name to reference the function in SQL statements. The function name must be globally unique and cannot be changed after the function is registered. |
| Owner | This parameter is automatically specified. |

The required resources are uploaded.

**Procedure**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Write Java code in the offline Java environment, compress the code to a JAR package, and
upload the package as a JAR resource to DataWorks. For more information, see Create, reference, and download resources.
3. Create a function.
i. Find the workflow that you want to use, right-click **MaxCompute**, and then select **Create**

iii. On the **Register Function** tab, configure the following parameters.

| Class Name | Required. The name of the class that implements the function. Note If the resource type is Python, enter the class name in the Python resource name.Class name format. Do not include the .py extension in the resource name. |
|---|---|
| Resources | Required. You can perform a fuzzy match to search for existing resources in the current workspace. |
| Description | The description of the function. |
| Expression Syntax | The syntax of the function. Example: test . |
| Parameter Description | The description of the input and output parameters that are supported. |
| Return Value | Optional. The return value. Example: 1. |
| Example | Optional. An example of the function. |

4. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the function.
5. Commit the function.
i. Click the icon in the top toolbar to commit the function. ii. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. iii. Click **OK**.
