##### Create a node to synchronize schemas of

**MaxCompute tables**

DataWorks provides the table schema import feature. This feature allows you to create multiple Hologres external tables whose schemas are the same as those of the source MaxCompute tables at a time. You can use the created Hologres external tables to accelerate data queries on the source MaxCompute tables. This topic describes how to create a node to synchronize schemas of MaxCompute tables with a few clicks. A **Hologres** compute engine is added on the **Workspace Management** page. This ensures that the **Hologres** folder is displayed in the Scheduled Workflow pane. For more information, see the "Associate a Hologres compute engine instance with a workspace" section of the Configure a workspace topic.

**Step 1: Create a table schema synchronization node**

1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Destination Name | The name of the Hologres instance. |
| Destination Database | The name of the database in the Hologres instance. |
| Schema | The name of the schema in the database. |

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Type | The type of the source tables based on which you want to create Hologres external tables. Only MaxCompute is supported. |
| Servers | The server on which the source tables reside. You can use the odps server server that is created at the underlying _ layer of Hologres. For more information, see postgres fdw. _ |
| Source Project | The name of the project to which the source tables belong. |

iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Find the workflow in which you want to create a Hologres node, right-click Hologres, and
then choose **Create Node > Hologres > Schema Synchronization from**
**MaxCompute**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Configure the table schema synchronization node**

On the configuration tab of the node, configure the Hologres connection information for the Hologres external tables, the source information of the MaxCompute tables, and the policy that is used to handle conflicts that may occur when you create the Hologres external tables.
1. Configure the information about the destination.
You can configure the parameters to specify the Hologres instance in which you want to store the Hologres external tables.
2. Configure the information about the source.
You can configure the parameters to specify the source MaxCompute tables based on which you create Hologres external tables. DataWorks allows you to create Hologres external tables whose schemas are the same as those of the source MaxCompute tables based on the parameters that you configure. Then, you can use the created Hologres external tables to accelerate data queries on the source MaxCompute tables.

| er Guide·DataStudio | DataWork |
|---|---|

| Select Tables For Query Acceleration | The source tables based on which you want to create Hologres external tables. Valid values: All Tables in Database: All tables in the selected project. Selected Tables: Specific tables in the selected project. If you select this option, you can search for tables by name. Note Fuzzy match is supported. After you enter a keyword, all tables whose names contain the keyword are displayed. |
|---|---|

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Action for Table Name Conflicts | The policy that is used to handle the following conflict: The name of the Hologres external table that you want to create is the same as the name of an existing Hologres table. Valid values: Ignore Conflicts and Continue Creating Tables Update and Change Names of Tables with Same Names Report Error and Create No Table |
| Data Type Not Supported | The policy that is used to handle the following conflict: The data type of the Hologres external table that you want to create is not supported by Hologres. Valid values: Report Error and Import Failed: If you select this option, the Hologres external table fails to be created. Ignore and Skip Unsupported Fields: If you select this option, the system skips fields whose data types are not supported and continues to create the Hologres external table. |

3. Configure the policy that is used to handle conflicts.
The parameters that you configure in this section determine the policy that is used to handle conflicts that may occur when you create the Hologres external tables.

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node.

**Step 4: Run node code**

You can perform the following operations to check whether the node is configured as expected based on your business requirements:
1. Optional. Select a resource group and assign custom parameters to variables.
Click the icon in the top toolbar of the configuration tab of the node. In the
**Parameters** dialog box, select a resource group for scheduling that you want to use to
debug and run node code. If you use scheduling parameters in your node code, assign the scheduling parameters to variables as values in the node code for debugging.
2. Save and run node code.
In the top toolbar, click the icon to save node code and click the icon to run node code.

##### Create a node to synchronize data from

#### MaxCompute

DataWorks allows you to create a node to synchronize data from MaxCompute to Hologres with a few clicks on the DataStudio page. This way, you can accelerate data queries on MaxCompute tables. This topic describes how to create a node to synchronize data from MaxCompute to Hologres with a few clicks. A **Hologres** compute engine is added on the **Workspace Management** page. This ensures that the **Hologres** folder is displayed in the Scheduled Workflow pane. For more information, see the "Associate a Hologres compute engine instance with a workspace" section of the Configure a workspace topic.

**Step 1: Create a data synchronization node**

1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Find the workflow in which you want to create a Hologres node, right-click Hologres, and
then choose **Create Node > Hologres > Data Synchronization from MaxCompute** .
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Configure the data synchronization node**

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Destination Name | The name of the Hologres instance on which the Hologres external table resides. |
| Destination Database | The name of the database in which the Hologres external table resides in the Hologres instance. |
| Source of External Table | The source of the Hologres external table. The Hologres external table is mapped to the source MaxCompute table and used to synchronize data from the source MaxCompute table to a Hologres internal table. Valid values: Existing External Table: You can select this option if the Hologres external table that you want to use already exists. If you select this option, you must specify the schema and name of the Hologres external table. Create External Table: You must select this option if no Hologres external table that is mapped to the source MaxCompute table exists. If you select this option, you must specify the server that is used by the Hologres external table, the name of the MaxCompute project to which the source MaxCompute table belongs, and the name of the source MaxCompute table. Note You can use the odps server server that is created at the _ underlying layer of Hologres. For more information, see postgres fdw. _ |

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Destination Schema | The schema to which the Hologres internal table belongs. |

On the configuration tab of the node, configure the information about the source MaxCompute table from which you want to synchronize data, the information about the destination table to which you want to store the synchronized data, the data synchronization policy, and the SQL statement.
1. Configure the information about the source MaxCompute table.
You can configure the parameters to specify the source MaxCompute table from which you want to synchronize data. In this section, you must configure the information about the Hologres external table that is mapped to the source MaxCompute table. The following table describes the parameters.
2. Configure the destination Hologres internal table.
You can configure the parameters to create a Hologres internal table in which you want to store the synchronized data.

| Target Table | The name of the Hologres internal table. If the name of the Hologres internal table that you specify already exists, Hologres processes the existing internal table based on the following policies: Non-partitioned table: Hologres deletes the existing internal table and creates another internal table with the same name. Partitioned table: Hologres does not delete the existing internal table. Hologres creates partitions in the table based on partition values and synchronizes data to the new partitions. Note An error is reported if the schema of the created internal table is different from that of the existing internal table with the same name. |
|---|---|
| Destination Table Description | The description of the Hologres internal table. |

| Tab | Description |
|---|---|
| Synchronization Field | Select the fields in the source MaxCompute table from which you want to synchronize data. |
| Partition Configurations | Select the partitions in the source MaxCompute table from which you want to synchronize data. Note Hologres allows you to synchronize data only from level-1 partitions in the source MaxCompute table. If the source MaxCompute table contains multiple levels of partitions, you must specify the level-1 partition field of the source MaxCompute table for the destination table. Other partition fields in the source MaxCompute table are mapped to common fields in the destination table. |
| Index Configuration | Configure an index for the Hologres internal table to store the synchronized MaxCompute data. You can accelerate data queries by using the index. |

3. Configure the synchronization policy.
You can configure the parameters to configure the synchronization policy.
4. Generate an SQL script.
DataWorks parses the SQL statement that is used to run the current data synchronization node based on the synchronization configurations. You can go to the code editor of Hologres and run the data synchronization node in SQL mode.

**Note**

You cannot modify the generated SQL script. If the configurations of the data synchronization node are changed, you can click Refresh to generate a new SQL statement.

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node.

**Step 4: Debug node code**

You can perform the following operations to check whether the node is configured as expected based on your business requirements:
1. Optional. Select a resource group and assign custom parameters to variables.
Click the icon in the top toolbar of the configuration tab of the node. In the
**Parameters** dialog box, select a resource group for scheduling that you want to use to
debug and run the node code. If you use scheduling parameters in your node code, assign the scheduling parameters to variables as values in the node code for debugging.
2. Save and run node code.
In the top toolbar, click the icon to save node code and click the icon to run node code. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. In the top toolbar, click the
icon to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. If you use a workspace in standard mode, you must deploy the node to the production environment after you commit the node. To deploy a node, click **Deploy** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the node. For more information, see Deploy nodes.

**What to do next**

Task O&M: After you commit and deploy the node, the node is periodically run based on the scheduling configurations. You can click **Operation Center** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the corresponding node to go to Operation Center and view the scheduling status of the node. For more information, see Auto triggered node O&M.

##### CDH Hive node

If you have a deployed CDH cluster and want to run Hive tasks such as data query jobs or batch data processing in DataWorks, you can use a CDH Hive node. This topic describes how to create a CDH Hive node. The **CDH** directory appears only after you add a **CDH** compute engine instance on the
**Workspace Configurations** page. For more information, see Bind a CDH compute engine.

i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the target workflow and choose **New Node > CDH > CDH Hive**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Develop a CDH Hive task**

After the node is created, write your code. For example:

```
show tables; select * from userinfo ;
```

You can perform smoke testing on the node in the development environment when you commit the node or after you commit the node. For more information, see Perform smoke testing. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. In the top toolbar, click the
icon to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. ##### CDH Spark node

Spark is a general-purpose big data analytics engine known for its high performance, ease of use, and versatility. It enables complex in-memory analytics and helps you build large-scale, low-latency data analysis applications. DataWorks provides CDH Spark nodes for developing and periodically scheduling Spark jobs. This topic describes how to create and use a CDH Spark node. The **CDH** directory appears only after you add a **CDH** compute engine instance on the
**workspace configuration** page. For more information, see Bind a CDH compute engine.
1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the target workflow and select **Create Node > CDH > CDH Spark**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Develop the CDH Spark job**

In the CDH Spark node you created, you can reference a JAR resource, write your code, and submit the job by using the spark-submit command.
1. Create a CDH JAR resource.
In the corresponding workflow, right-click **CDH > Resource** and select **Create Resource**
**> CDH JAR**. In the **Create Resource** dialog box, click **Upload** and select the file to upload.
2. Reference the CDH JAR resource.
i. Open the CDH node that you created. The editor page opens. ii. Under **CDH > Resource**, find the resource to reference (for example, `spark-` `examples_2.11_2.4.0.jar` ), right-click the resource name, and select **Reference**
**Resource**.
After you **reference the resource**, if a statement in the format of
##@resource_reference{""} appears in the code editor for the CDH node, it indicates that
you successfully referenced the resource. The following is an example:

```
##@resource_reference{"spark_examples_2.11_2.4.0.jar"}
spark_examples_2.11_2.4.0.jar
```

3. Modify the CDH Spark node code to add the spark-submit command. The following is a
modified example.

**Important**

Comments are not supported when editing code for a CDH Spark node. To prevent runtime errors, modify the job code as shown in the following example and remove all comments.

```
##@resource_reference{"spark-examples_2.11-2.4.0.jar"}
spark-submit --class org.apache.spark.examples.SparkPi --master yarn sparkexamples_2.11-2.4.0.jar 100
```

The following describes the parameters:
**org.apache.spark.examples.SparkPi**: The main class of the job in the JAR package.
**spark-examples_2.11-2.4.0.jar**: The name of the CDH JAR resource you uploaded.

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node.

**Step 4: Debug the node code**

You can perform the following operations to check whether the node is configured as expected based on your business requirements:
1. Optional. Select a resource group and assign scheduling parameters to variables.
Click the icon in the top toolbar of the configuration tab of the node. In the
**Parameters** dialog box, select a resource group for scheduling that you want to use to
debug the code. If you use scheduling parameters in your code, assign the scheduling parameters to variables as values in the node code for debugging.
2. Save and run the code.
In the top toolbar, click the icon to save node code and click the icon to run node code.
3. Optional. Perform smoke testing.
You can perform smoke testing on the node in the development environment when you commit the node or after you commit the node. For more information, see Perform smoke testing. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. In the top toolbar, click the
icon to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. If you use a workspace in standard mode, you must deploy the node to the production environment after you commit the node. To deploy a node, click **Deploy** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the node. For more information, see Deploy nodes.

**What to do next**

Task O&M: After you commit and deploy the node, the node is periodically run based on the scheduling configurations. You can click **Operation Center** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the corresponding node to go to Operation Center and view the scheduling status of the node. For more information, see Auto triggered node O&M.

##### CDH MR node

In DataWorks, you can create a CDH MR (MapReduce) node to process large-scale datasets. The **CDH** directory is displayed only after you add a **CDH** compute engine instance on the
**Workspace Configuration** page. For more information, see Bind a CDH compute engine.
1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the target workflow and choose **New Node > CDH > CDH MR**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Develop a CDH MR task**

In DataWorks, you can upload resources from your local machine to Data Development and reference them in your task.
1. Create a CDH JAR resource.
In the corresponding workflow, right-click **CDH > Resources** and choose **New Resource**
**> CDH JAR**. In the **New Resource** dialog box, **click to upload** your file.
2. Reference the CDH JAR resource.
i. Open the **CDH MR** node that you created. The node editor opens. ii. Under **CDH > Resources**, find the resource that you want to reference, for example, `onaliyun_mr_wordcount-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar` . Right-click the resource name and choose
**Reference Resource**.
3. After you select **Reference Resource**, a statement in the format
##@resource_reference{""} is added to the code editor, which indicates that the resource
is referenced. Run the following command to execute the task. The resource package, bucket name, and path in the following command are examples. Replace them with your actual information.

```
##@resource_reference{"onaliyun_mr_wordcount-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar"}
onaliyun_mr_wordcount-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar cn.apache.hadoop.onaliyun.examples.EmrWordCount oss://onaliyun-bucket- 2/cdh/datas/wordcount02/inputs oss://onaliyun-bucket-2/cdh/datas/wordcount02/outputs
```

**Note**

The CDH MR node code editor does not support comments.

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

debug the code. If you use scheduling parameters in your code, assign the scheduling parameters to variables as values in the node code for debugging.
2. Save and run the code.
In the top toolbar, click the icon to save node code and click the icon to run node code.
3. Optional. Perform smoke testing.
You can perform smoke testing on the node in the development environment when you commit the node or after you commit the node. For more information, see Perform smoke testing. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. In the top toolbar, click the
icon to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. ##### CDH Impala nodes

In DataWorks, you can use Cloudera's Distribution Including Apache Hadoop (CDH) Impala nodes to write and run Impala SQL scripts. CDH Impala nodes provide higher query performance than CDH Hive nodes. This topic describes how to create and use a CDH Impala node. On the **Workspace Management** page, a **CDH** compute engine instance is associated with the workspace that you want to use. After that, the **CDH** folder appears. For more information, see the "Associate a CDH compute engine instance with a workspace" section of the Configure a workspace topic.

**Step 1: Create a CDH Impala node**

1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the workflow that you want to manage and choose **Create Node > CDH > CDH**
**Impala**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Use the CDH Impala node to develop a task**

After the CDH Impala node is created, edit the code of the node. The code must conform to the syntax. Example:

```
show tables; select * from userinfo ;
```

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node.

**Step 4: Debug the node code**

You can perform the following operations to check whether the node is configured as expected based on your business requirements:
1. Optional. Select a resource group and assign scheduling parameters to variables.
Click the icon in the top toolbar of the configuration tab of the node. In the
**Parameters** dialog box, select a resource group for scheduling that you want to use to
debug the code. If you use scheduling parameters in your code, assign the scheduling parameters to variables as values in the node code for debugging.
2. Save and run the code.
In the top toolbar, click the icon to save node code and click the icon to run node code.
3. Optional. Perform smoke testing.
You can perform smoke testing on the node in the development environment when you commit the node or after you commit the node. For more information, see Perform smoke testing. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. In the top toolbar, click the
icon to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. If you use a workspace in standard mode, you must deploy the node to the production environment after you commit the node. To deploy a node, click **Deploy** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the node. For more information, see Deploy nodes.

**What to do next**

Task O&M: After you commit and deploy the node, the node is periodically run based on the scheduling configurations. You can click **Operation Center** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the corresponding node to go to Operation Center and view the scheduling status of the node. For more information, see Auto triggered node O&M.

##### Create an AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL table

This topic describes how to create an AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL table. On the **Workspace Management** page, an AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL compute engine instance is associated with the workspace in which you want to create an AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL table. After that, the AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL folder appears. For more information, see the Associate an AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL compute engine instance section in the "Configure a workspace" topic. The metadata of the associated AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL instance is collected on the
**Data Map** page. For more information, see Collect metadata from an AnalyticDB for
PostgreSQL data source.

**Step 1: Create an AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL table**

1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the workflow that you want to manage and choose **Create Table > AnalyticDB**
**for PostgreSQL > Table**.
3. In the **Create Table** dialog box, enter a name in the **Name** field.

**Important**

The table name must be in the format of **schema_name.table_name**. The values of **schema_name** and **table_name** must be 1 to 63 characters in length and can contain letters, digits, and underscores (_). The values must start with a letter or underscore (_). If you associate multiple AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL instances with the current workspace, you must select one based on your business requirements.
4. Click **Create**. The configuration tab of the table appears.
The upper part of the table configuration tab displays the **table name** and **AnalyticDB for**
**PostgreSQL instance name**.

**Step 2: Configure the AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL table**

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Level-1 Theme | The name of the level-1 folder in which the table resides. Note The level-1 and level-2 folders show the table locations in DataWorks to help you easily manage tables. |
| Level-2 Theme | The name of the level-2 folder in which the table resides. |
| Create Folder | Click Create Folder to go to the Folder Management tab. On the Folder Management tab, you can create level-1 and level-2 folders. After you create a folder, click the icon. |
| Descriptio n | The description of the table. |

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Level | The layer where the table data is stored or processed. A data warehouse consists of the operational data store (ODS), common data model (CDM), and application data service (ADS) layers. You can specify a name for each layer. |
| Category | The business category to which the table belongs. Tables are categorized into the basic, advanced, and other-purpose business categories. You can specify a name for each business category. Note Business categories are designed only to help you manage the table and do not affect underlying implementation. |
| Create Level | The layers and business categories that you want to create. To create layers and business categories, click Create Level to go to the Level Management tab. After you create levels and business categories, click the icon. |

1. In the **General** section, configure the parameters.
2. In the **Physical Model** section, configure the parameters.
3. In the **Schema** section, configure the parameters.

| Tab | Parameter | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Column information settings | New columns | Click the button and configure the relevant parameters to create a field. |
|  | Name | The name of the field. |
|  | Field type | The data type of the field. |
|  | Field length | The length of the field. You can specify the length for fields only of specific data types. |
|  | Default value | The default value of the field. |
|  | Allow to be empty | Specifies whether the field can be empty. |
|  | Primary key | Specifies whether the field serves as the primary key. |
|  | Unique key | Specifies whether the field serves as the unique key. |
|  | Actions | You can perform the following operations on a new field: save, cancel, delete, move up, and move down. You can perform the following operations on an existing field: modify, delete, move up, and move down. |
| Index settings | New columns | Click the button and configure the relevant parameters to create an index. |
|  | Index name | The name of the index. Make sure that you specify a unique name. |
|  | Include columns | The field on which the index will be created. To select a field, click Edit. In the Select at least one index dialog box, click the + icon. All the created fields appear in the Column information drop-down list. Select the field from the Column information drop-down list and click Save. |
|  | Index type | The type of the index. Valid values: Normal, Primary Key, and Unique. |

You can configure the schema of an AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL table on the following tabs:
**Column information settings**, **Index settings**, **Sub-table design**, and **Partition**
**settings (optional)**.

|  | Index mode | The mode for indexing data in the fields. Valid values: B- tree, Bitmap, and GiST. |
|---|---|---|
|  | Actions | You can perform the following operations on a new index: save, cancel, delete, move up, and move down. You can perform the following operations on an existing index: modify, delete, move up, and move down. |
| Sub-table design | Hash (Recommended), Copy Schema, and Random (Not Recommended) | The way in which the partition key is generated. Take Hash (Recommended) as an example. Click New columns and select the target field from the Name drop- down list. The information about the selected field appears. Click Save. For more information, see the Column information settings section of this table. |
| Partition settings (optional) | Partition settings (optional) | The partitions of the table. You can configure the partitions based on your business requirements. |

1. Click **Submit to development environment** and **Submit to production environment**
in sequence. If you are using a workspace in basic mode, you need to only click **Submit to production**
**environment**.
2. In the **Submit changes** dialog box, confirm that the table creation statements are correct,
select a resource group from the **Select a resource group** drop-down list, and then click
**Confirm execution**.

**What to do next**

After the AnalyticDB for PostgreSQL table is created, you can query data in the table and modify or delete the table. For more information, see Manage tables.

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the target Business Process and choose **Create Node > database > Oracle**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Develop an Oracle task**

1. If your workspace has multiple Oracle data sources, select the desired data source on the
editor page of the Oracle node. If only one Oracle data source exists, it is used by default.
2. On the node's editor page, write code that complies with Oracle syntax.

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node.

**Step 4: Debug the node code**

You can perform the following operations to check whether the node is configured as expected based on your business requirements:
1. Optional. Select a resource group and assign scheduling parameters to variables.
Click the icon in the top toolbar of the configuration tab of the node. In the
**Parameters** dialog box, select a resource group for scheduling that you want to use to
debug the code. If you use scheduling parameters in your code, assign the scheduling parameters to variables as values in the node code for debugging.
2. Save and run the code.
In the top toolbar, click the icon to save node code and click the icon to run node code.
3. Optional. Perform smoke testing.
You can perform smoke testing on the node in the development environment when you commit the node or after you commit the node. For more information, see Perform smoke testing. After the node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system periodically runs tasks on the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. In the top toolbar, click the
icon to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. If you use a workspace in standard mode, you must deploy the node to the production environment after you commit the node. To deploy a node, click **Deploy** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the node. For more information, see Deploy nodes.

**What to do next**

Task O&M: After you commit and deploy the node, the node is periodically run based on the scheduling configurations. You can click **Operation Center** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the corresponding node to go to Operation Center and view the scheduling status of the node. For more information, see Auto triggered node O&M.

#### General

##### For-each node

###### Logic of for-each nodes

DataWorks provides for-each nodes that are used to loop through the dataset passed by an assignment node. You can also orchestrate the inner workflow of a for-each node. This topic describes the composition and application logic of a for-each node.

**Instructions for use**

The following table describes the instructions for use of for-each nodes.

| Learn the limits and usage notes of for-each nodes, such as the upper limit for the number of loops, the method to test a for-each node, and the method to view logs of a for-each node. | Limits Usage notes |
|---|---|
| Learn that you can customize an inner workflow for a for-each node based on your business requirements. During customization, make sure that the start node and end node of the inner workflow must be provided by the for-each node. | Node composition and workflow orchestration |
| Learn that the number of loops for a for-each node is determined by the output of an assignment node. | Number of loops |
| Learn that the built-in variables provided by a for-each node can be used to obtain the related values from the dataset of an assignment node in each loop. | Built-in variables |
| Learn samples of variable values and the number of loops for a for-each node. | Examples of variable values |

**Use scenario**

A for-each node in DataWorks is used in loop traversal scenarios and must be used with an assignment node. An assignment node must be configured as the ancestor node of a for-each node. After the assignment node passes its output to the for-each node, the for-each node loops through the output.

**Limits**

The maximum number of loops for a for-each node is 1024. The actual number of loops for a for-each node is determined by the dataset passed by an assignment node. Parallel execution is not supported. A loop can start only if the previous loop ends.

**Usage notes**

| Dimensio n | Item | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Dependenc ies | Dependency settings | A for-each node needs to loop through the values passed by an assignment node. Therefore, an assignment node must be configured as the ancestor node of a for-each node. The for-each node must depend on the assignment node. |
| Loops | Maximum number of loops | The maximum number of loops for a for-each node is 1024. If the number of loops for a for-each node exceeds 1024, an error is reported. The actual number of loops for a for-each node is determined by the output of an assignment node. |
|  | Number of loops | The number of loops for a for-each node is determined by the dataset passed by an assignment node. |
| Inner nodes | Workflow orchestratio n | You can delete the existing dependencies between inner nodes of a for-each node and customize an inner workflow for the for-each node based on your business requirements. During customization, make sure that the start node and end node of the inner workflow must be provided by the for-each node. If a branch node is used as the inner node of a for-each node to perform a logical judgment or loop through the dataset of an assignment node, a merge node is also required. |
|  | Value acquisition | The built-in variables provided by a for-each node can be used to obtain a specific value passed by the assignment node that is configured as the ancestor node of the for-each node. |
| Debugging | Task debugging | If you use a workspace in standard mode, you cannot directly perform a test to run a for-each node in DataStudio. If you want to verify the running result of a for-each node, you must commit and deploy the task that contains the for-each node to Operation Center in the development environment and run the for- each node. You need to run the assignment node and for-each node at the same time. When you backfill data for an auto triggered node in Operation Center, start the data backfill from the assignment node and run both the assignment node and the for-each node. Do not run the for- each node separately. |
|  | Log viewing | To view the operation logs of a for-each node in Operation Center, perform the following steps: Find the for-each node on the Cycle Task page and open the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the node. In the DAG, right-click the node name and select View Internal Nodes to view the operation logs of the inner nodes. |

**Node composition and workflow orchestration**

A for-each node is a type of special node that contains inner nodes. When you create a foreach node, the following three inner nodes are automatically created: **start node**, **Shell**
**node**, and **end node**. The start node marks the start of each loop. The Shell node specifies
the task. Multiple types of nodes are supported, and the Shell node is for reference only. The end node marks the end of a loop. The inner nodes are organized into an inner workflow to loop through the output of the upstream assignment node. The preceding figure shows the following information: DataWorks automatically creates an ODPS SQL node for node execution. You can delete this default node and configure an inner node for node execution based on your business requirements. If a Shell node is used for the loop task, you can place it between the start and end nodes, and configure the dependencies. Then, double-click the **Shell node** to go to the code development page of the node to develop the task code. If the for-each node is complicated, you can add other nodes to the for-each node to orchestrate the inner workflow based on your business requirements.

**Note**

When you customize inner nodes of a for-each node, you can delete the dependencies between existing inner nodes and orchestrate the inner workflow. Make sure that the inner workflow starts with the **start node** and ends with the **end**
**node**.
**Start node** and **end node**
The start node marks the start of a loop, and the end node marks the end of a loop. The two nodes are not used to process a loop task.

**Note**

The number of loops for a for-each node is determined by the output of an assignment node rather than the end node.

**Number of loops**

|  | Built-in variable |  | Description | Compare with the for loop |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|  | ${dag.loopDa taArray} |  | Obtains the dataset of an assignment node. | Equivalent to the code result in the for loop. data=[] |
|  |  | ${dag.loopDa | dataset |  |
|  | taArray} |  |  |  |

**Note**

The maximum number of loops for a for-each node is 1024. The actual number of loops for a for-each node is determined by the dataset passed by an assignment node. The number of loops is determined based on the following logic: For assignment nodes that use Shell or Python syntax: The number of loops is the number of elements in the one-dimensional array output. The elements are separated by commas (,). For example, if the assignment node is a Shell node or Python (Python 2) node and the output is the one-dimensional array `2021-03-28,2021-03-29,2021-03-30,2021-03-31,2021-04-` `01` , the for-each node loops through the output of the assignment node for five times. For assignment nodes that use SQL syntax: The number of loops is the number of rows in the two-dimensional array output. For example, if the assignment node is an ODPS SQL node and the output is the following two-dimensional array:

```
+----------------------------------------------+
| uid            | region | age_range | zodiac |
+----------------------------------------------+
| 0016359810821  | Hubei Province | 30 to 40 years old   | Cancer |
| 0016359814159  | Unknown   | 30 to 40 years old   | Cancer |
+----------------------------------------------+
```

The for-each node loops through the output of the assignment node twice.

**Built-in variables**

You can use the built-in variables provided by a for-each node to obtain the dataset passed by the assignment node that is configured as the ancestor node of the for-each node. If the inner workflow for the for-each node contains an assignment node, the descendant node of the assignment node obtains the output of this assignment node by default. For more information, see Assignment node. You can use the built-in variables provided by a for-each node to obtain the number of loops that are finished and the offset between the current loop and the first loop when the for-each node is used to loop through the output of the assignment node.

###### Configure a for-each node

DataWorks provides for-each nodes that are used to loop through the dataset passed by an assignment node. You can also orchestrate the inner workflow of a for-each node. This topic describes how to create a for-each node and use it to develop a task. Before you configure a for-each node, you must be familiar with the logic of a for-each node. This prevents errors during the configuration of the node. For more information, see Logic of for-each nodes.
1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the workflow that you want to manage and choose **Create Node > General >**
**for-each**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.
1. Double-click the workflow that you created to go to the configuration tab of the workflow.
Create an assignment node as the ancestor of the for-each node. Double-click the assignment node to go to the configuration tab of the node.
2. Set the Language parameter to Shell for the assignment node and enter the following code:

```
echo 'this is name,ok';
```

On the node configuration tab, click the **Properties** tab in the right-side navigation pane. By default, the **outputs** parameter appears in the **Output Parameters** section.
3. Find the for-each node that you created and replace the node between the `start` and
`end` nodes with the Shell node.
4. Double-click the Shell node and write the following code:

```
echo ${dag.loopTimes} ---- Displays the number of loops.
```

**Note**

The start and end nodes of the for-each node have fixed logic and cannot be modified. After you modify the code of the Shell node, you must save the modification. The system does not prompt you to save the modification when you commit the node. If you do not save the modification, the code cannot be updated to the latest version in time. For more information about the built-in variables supported by the for-each node, see Builtin variables.
5. Return to the configuration tab of the for-each node and click Properties in the right-side
navigation pane. Find the parameter named `loopDataArray` under **Input Parameters** in the **Input and Output Parameters** section. Click **Change** in the Actions column. Change the value in the **Value Source** field and click **Save** in the **Actions** column. The value in the **Parameter Name** field is fixed to `loopDataArray` and cannot be modified. Select the outputs parameter of the ancestor assignment node for **Value Source**.
6. Click the **Save** icon in the top toolbar of the for-each node.

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. After a for-each node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system runs the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Switch to the workflow configuration tab and click the
icon in the toolbar to commit the workflow.
2. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine
whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. If you use a workspace in standard mode, you must deploy the node to the production environment after you commit the node. To deploy a node, click **Deploy** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the node. For more information, see Deploy nodes.

**Step 5: Test the for-each node and view test results**

The procedure for committing, deploying, and running a for-each node is the same as that for a common node. However, you cannot test a for-each node in DataStudio.

**Note**

If you want to verify the running result of a for-each node, you must commit and deploy the task that contains the for-each node to Operation Center and run the for-each node in Operation Center. If you use the values passed by an assignment node that serves as the ancestor of the for-each node, run both the assignment node and the for-each node in Operation Center.
1. On the node configuration tab, click **Operation Center** in the upper-right corner to go to
**Operation Center**.
2. In the left-side navigation pane of the Operation Center page, choose **Cycle Task**
**Maintenance > Cycle Task**.
3. On the Cycle Task page, find the for-each node and click DAG in the Actions column to open
the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the for-each node. In the DAG of the for-each node, right-click the assignment node and choose **Run > Current and Descendant Nodes**
**Retroactively**.
4. In the Backfill Data pane, configure the **Select Descendant Tasks** and **Data Timestamp**
parameters and click **Submit and Redirect**. The system redirects to the **Patch Data** page.
5. Refresh the **Patch Data** page. After the data backfill instance is run, click **DAG** in the
Actions column of the instance.
6. In the DAG that appears, right-click the assignment node and select **View Runtime Log** to
view its operation logs.
7. On the **Patch Data** page, right-click the for-each node in the DAG and select **View**
**Internal Nodes**.
8. On the page that appears, click **Loop 1** in the middle pane, right-click the Shell node in the
DAG, and then select **View Runtime Log**. On the page that appears, view the operation logs of the Shell node in the first loop.
9. Use the same method to view the operation logs of the Shell node in the second loop.

You can click **Operation Center** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the corresponding node to go to Operation Center and view the scheduling status of the node. For more information, see Auto triggered node O&M.

##### Do-while nodes

###### Logic of do-while nodes

DataWorks provides do-while nodes. You can rearrange the workflow inside a do-while node, write the logic to be executed in a loop in the node, and then configure an end node to determine whether to exit from looping. You can use a do-while node alone, or use a do-while node together with an assignment node to loop through the result set passed by the assignment node. This topic describes the composition and application logic of a do-while node.

**Background information**

The following table describes the instructions for use of do-while nodes.

| Dimension | Item | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Loops | Maximum number of loops | The maximum number of loops for a do-while node is 1024. If the number of loops for a do-while node exceeds 1024, an error is reported. The actual number of loops for a do-while node is determined by the end node. |
| Inner nodes | Workflow orchestration | You can delete the existing dependencies between inner nodes of a do-while node and customize an inner workflow for the do-while node based on your business requirements. During customization, make sure that the start node and end node of the inner workflow must be provided by the do-while node. If a branch node is used as the inner node of a do-while node to perform a logical judgment or loop, a merge node is also required. You cannot add comments when you write the code of thee nd node of a do-while node. |
|  | Value acquisition | The built-in variables provided by a do-while node can be used to obtain a specific value passed by the assignment node that is configured as the ancestor node of the do-while node. |
| Debugging | Node debugging | If you use a workspace in standard mode, you cannot directly perform a test to run a do-while node in DataStudio. If you want to verify the running result of a do-while node, you must commit and deploy the task that contains the do-while node to Operation Center in the development environment and run the do- while node. |
|  | Log viewing | To view the operation logs of a do-while node in Operation Center, perform the following steps: Find the do-while node on the Cycle Task page and open the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the node. In the DAG, right-click the node name and select View Internal Nodes to view the operation logs of the inner nodes. |
| Dependencie s | Dependency settings | You can use a do-while node separately or together with an assignment node. If you want to check whether an assignment node passes its output to a do-while node in Operation Center, you can use the data backfill feature to backfill data for both the assignment node and do-while node. If you run only the do-while node, you cannot obtain the output of the assignment node. |

**Limits**

The maximum number of loops for a do-while node is 1024. Parallel execution is not supported. A loop can start only if the previous loop ends.

**Usage notes**

**Node composition and workflow orchestration**

A do-while node is a type of special node that contains inner nodes. When you create a dowhile node, the following three inner nodes are automatically created: **start node**, **Shell**
**node**, and **end node**. The start node marks the start of each loop. The Shell node specifies
the task. Multiple types of nodes are supported, and the Shell node is for reference only. The end node judges the ending of a loop. The inner nodes are organized into an inner workflow to run the do-while node in loops. The preceding figure shows the following information:

**Start node**

The start node marks the start of a loop and does not contain any code. All inner nodes of a do-while node depend on the start node. Therefore, the start node cannot be deleted.

**Looping logic**

When you create a do-while node, DataWorks automatically creates an inner ODPS SQL node to process the looping logic. You can delete the default node and configure inner nodes based on your business requirements. In most cases, a do-while node is used together with an assignment node, a branch node and a merge node. When you customize inner nodes of a do-while node, you can delete the dependencies between existing inner nodes and orchestrate the inner workflow. Make sure that the inner workflow starts with the **start node** and ends with the **end node**.

**End node**

The **end node** determines whether to exit from looping. The end node can control the number of loops that can be run for the do-while node. The end node is essentially an assignment node. The end node returns `True` to run the next loop or `False` to exit from looping. You can use ODPS SQL, Shell, or Python 2 to write code for the **end node**. The do-while node provides built-in variables for you to write code for the end node. For more information about the built-in variables, see Built-in variables and Examples of variable values. For more information about sample code written in different languages, see Sample code for the end node. An inner node to be run in a specific loop must be the ancestor of the end node, and the end node cannot be deleted.

**Built-in variables**

| Built-in variable | Description | Value |
|---|---|---|
| ${dag.loopTimes} | The number of loops that are finished. | 1 for the first loop, 2 for the second loop, 3 for the third loop, ..., and n for the nth loop. |
| ${dag.offset} | The offset between the current loop and the previous loop. | 0 for the first loop, 1 for the second loop, 2 for the third loop, ..., and n-1 for the nth loop. |

| Built-in variable | Description |
|---|---|
| ${dag.input} | The dataset passed by the ancestor assignment node. |
| ${dag.input[${dag.offset}]} | The data entry obtained by the do-while node in the current loop. |
| ${dag.input.length} | The length of the dataset obtained by the do-while node. |

|  | ${dag.input[${dag.offset}]} |
|---|---|

In most cases, the built-in variables that are provided by a do-while node are configured in the **${dag.Variable name}** format. A do-while node in DataWorks provides two built-in variables **${dag.loopTimes}** and **${dag.offset}**. You can also use a do-while node together with an assignment node to obtain the values of the value assignment parameters based on built-in variables that are configured in the **${dag.Variable name}** format. Built-in system variables You can use the built-in variables provided by a do-while node to obtain the number of loops that are finished and the offset between loops when the do-while node is used for looping. Obtain the dataset passed by an assignment node If you use a do-while node together with an assignment node, you can obtain the values of the value assignment parameters and loop variables by using the built-in variables described in the following table.

**Note**

When the do-while node depends on an assignment node, you can add output parameters that are specified in **Output Parameters** for the assignment node to
**Input Parameters** for the do-while node. Then, you can use the do-while node to
obtain the dataset that is passed by the assignment node or specified content in the dataset. Input parameters are configured in the **${dag.Variable name}** format. Replace the **variable name** with the name of an input parameter that is specified in
**Input Parameters** for the do-while node. In the following built-in variables, `input`
specifies the name of the **input parameter** defined in the do-while node and is used to obtain the dataset that is passed by an assignment node. You must replace input with the actual name of the input parameter that you use.

| Built-in variable | Value for the first loop |  | Value for the second loop |
|---|---|---|---|
|  | 2021-03-28,2021-03-29,2021-03-30,2021-03-31,2021-04- 01 |  |  |
|  |  | 2021-03-28,2021-03-29,2021-03-30,2021-03-31,2021-04- |  |
| ${dag.input} | 01 |  |  |
| ${dag.input[${dag.offset}] } | 2021-03-28 |  | 2021-03-29 |
| ${dag.input.length} | 5 |  |  |
| ${dag.loopTimes} | 1 |  | 2 |
| ${dag.offset} | 0 |  | 1 |

|  | ${dag.input[${dag.offset}] |  |
|---|---|---|
| } |  |  |

The format of a dataset passed by an assignment node varies based on the language selected for the assignment node. If you use a do-while node to obtain the dataset that is passed by an assignment node and the assignment node uses the Shell language, the dataset or specified content in the dataset is passed to the do-while node as a **one-**
**dimensional array**. If the language selected for the assignment node is ODPS SQL, the
dataset or specified content in the dataset is passed to the do-while node as a **two-**
**dimensional array**. For more information, see Output format of the outputs parameter.

**Sample code for the end node**

You can use ODPS SQL, Shell, or Python 2 to write code for the **end node**. This section provides typical sample code in these languages.

**Use the ODPS SQL language**

| Usage notes | Configuration example |
|---|---|

```
 WHEN COUNT(1) > 0 AND ${dag.offset}<= 9
  THEN true
  ELSE false
 END
FROM xc_dpe_e2.xc_rpt_user_info_d where dt='20200101';
```

In the preceding sample code of the end node, the number of rows and the offset are compared with fixed values to limit the number of loops that can be run for the do-while node.

**Use the Shell language**

```
if [ ${dag.loopTimes} -lt 5 ]; then
     echo "True"
else
     echo "False"
```

`fi` In the preceding code, the number of loops that are finished is compared with 5 to limit the number of loops that can be run for the do-while node. The ${dag.loopTimes} variable specifies the number of loops that are finished. The value of the ${dag.loopTimes} variable is 1 for the first loop and increases by 1 each time. In this case, the value of the ${dag.loopTimes} variable is 2 for the second loop and 5 for the fifth loop. In the preceding sample code, when the fifth loop is finished, the output of the end node is False, and the do-while node exits from looping.

**Use the Python 2 language**

```bash
if ${dag.loopTimes}<${dag.input.length}:
   print True;
else
   print False;
# Start the next loop if the end node returns True.
# Exit from looping if the end node returns False.
```

In the preceding sample code, the number of loops that are finished is compared with the number of rows in the dataset passed by the assignment node to limit the number of loops that can be run for the do-while node. The ${dag.loopTimes} variable specifies the number of loops that are finished.

###### Configure a do-while node

DataWorks provides do-while nodes. You can rearrange the workflow inside a do-while node, write the logic to be executed in a loop in the node, and then configure an end node to determine whether to exit from looping. You can use a do-while node alone, or use a do-while node together with an assignment node to loop through the result set passed by the assignment node. This topic describes how to create a do-while node and use it to develop a task. Before you configure a do-while node, you must be familiar with the logic of a do-while node. This prevents errors during the configuration of the node. For more information, see Logic of do-while nodes.

**Step 1: Create a do-while node**

1. A workflow is created.
i. Log in to the DataWorks console. The DataStudio page appears by default. ii. In the **Scheduled Workflow** pane, right-click **Business Flow** and select **Create**
**Workflow**.
iii. In the **Create Workflow** dialog box, specify the **Workflow Name** and **Description** parameters. Then, click **Create**.

**Important**

The name of the workflow can be up to 128 characters in length.
2. Right-click the workflow that you want to manage and choose **Create Node > General >**
**do-while**.
3. In the **Create Node** dialog box, configure the **Name** parameter and click **Confirm**. Then,
you can use the node to develop and configure tasks.

**Step 2: Use the do-while node to develop a task**

1. Find the do-while node that you created and replace the node between the `start` and
`end` nodes with the Shell node.
2. Double-click the Shell node and write the following code:

```
echo ${dag.loopTimes} ---- Displays the number of loops.
```

The ${dag.loopTimes} variable is a reserved variable of the system. This variable specifies the current number of loops, and the value of this variable starts from 1. All inner nodes of the do-while node can reference this variable. For more information about the built-in variables, see Built-in variables and Examples of variable values. After you modify the code of the Shell node, save the modification. When you commit the node, no message appears to remind you to save the modification. If you do not save the modification, the code cannot be updated to the latest version in time.
3. Define the condition to exit the loop after the fifth iteration.
i. Return to the configuration tab of the do-while node. Double-click the inner end node to go to the configuration tab of the end node. ii. Select **Python** from the **Language** drop-down list. iii. Enter the following code to define the exit condition for the do-while loop:

```
if ${dag.loopTimes}<5:
 print True;
else:
 print False;
```

The ${dag.loopTimes} variable is a reserved variable of the system. This variable specifies the current number of loops, and the value of this variable starts from 1. All inner nodes of the do-while node can reference this variable. For more information about the built-in variables, see Built-in variables and Examples of variable values. In the code, the value of the `dag.loopTimes` variable is compared with 5 to limit the number of loops that can be run. The value of the ${dag.loopTimes} variable is 1 for the first loop, 2 for the second loop, and so on, until it reaches 5 for the fifth loop. The do-while node exits the loop when ${dag.loopTimes} < 5 evaluates to `False` .

**Step 3: Configure scheduling properties for the node**

If you want to periodically run the node, click **Properties** in the right-side navigation pane of the configuration tab of the node and configure the scheduling properties based on your business requirements. For more information, see Schedule.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. After a do-while node is configured, you must commit and deploy the node. After you commit and deploy the node, the system runs the node on a regular basis based on scheduling configurations.
1. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to save the node.
2. Click the
icon in the top toolbar to commit the node. In the **Submit** dialog box, configure the **Change description** parameter. Then, determine whether to review the node code after you commit the node based on your business requirements.

**Note**

You must configure the **Rerun** and **Parent Nodes** parameters on the Properties tab before you commit the node. You can use the code review feature to ensure the code quality of nodes and prevent execution errors caused by invalid node code. If you enable the code review feature, the node code that is committed can be deployed only after the node code passes the code review. For more information, see Code review. If you use a workspace in standard mode, you must deploy the node to the production environment after you commit the node. To deploy a node, click **Deploy** in the upper-right corner of the configuration tab of the node. For more information, see Deploy nodes.

**Step 5: Test the do-while node and view test results**

The procedure for committing, deploying, and running a do-while node is the same as that for committing, deploying, and running a common node. However, you cannot test a do-while node in DataStudio.

**Note**

If you want to verify the running result of a do-while node, you must commit and deploy the task that contains the do-while node to Operation Center and run the do-while node in Operation Center. If you use the values passed by an assignment node that serves as the ancestor of the do-while node, run both the assignment node and the do-while node in Operation Center.
1. On the configuration tab of the do-while node, click **Operation Center** in the top toolbar to
go to **Operation Center**.
2. In the left-side navigation pane of the Operation Center page, choose **Cycle Task**
**Maintenance > Cycle Task**.
3. On the Cycle Task page, find the do-while node and click DAG in the Actions column to
open the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the do-while node. In the DAG of the do-while node, right-click the assignment node and choose **Run > Current and Descendant**
**Nodes Retroactively**.
4. In the Backfill Data pane, configure the **Select Descendant Tasks** and **Data Timestamp**
parameters and click **Submit and Redirect**. The system redirects to the **Patch Data** page.
5. Refresh the **Patch Data** page. After the data backfill instance is run, click **DAG** in the
Actions column of the instance.
6. On the **Patch Data** page, right-click the do-while node in the DAG and select **View**
**Internal Nodes**.
7. On the page that appears, click **Loop 1** in the middle pane, right-click the Shell node in the
DAG, and then select **View Runtime Log**. On the page that appears, view the operation logs of the Shell node in the first loop.
8. Use the same method to view the operation logs of the Shell node in the second to fifth
loops and check whether the results meet your expectations. Comparison between a do-while node and the while, for-each, and do...while statement: A do-while node runs based on a workflow that starts a loop before evaluation. This node functions in the same way as the do...while statement. A do-while node can use the builtin variable ${dag.offset} and input and output parameters to achieve the feature of the for-each node. A do-while node cannot achieve the feature of the while statement because a do-while node runs a loop before evaluation. How does a do-while node work: i. The system runs a loop from the start node and runs other inner nodes based on the dependencies configured for them. ii. After the system runs the code that is defined for the end node in a loop, one of the following situations occurs: If the end node returns True, the loop runs again. If the end node returns False, the loop is terminated. Input and output parameters: The inner nodes of a do-while node can reference the input and output parameters of the do-while node by using the **${dag.Parameter name}** format. Built-in variables: DataWorks provides the following built-in variables for the inner nodes of the do-while node:
**dag.loopTimes**: the number of loops that are run. The value of this variable starts from
1.
**dag.offset**: the offset of the current loop iteration relative to the first one. The value of
this variable starts from 0.
